finding.claim: Any authenticated user can delete any project by id: the DELETE route calls the non-throwing boolean predicate authorized() and discards its result, so the ownership check never blocks the delete. High confidence.
finding.source: req.params.id (line 17), supplied by the calling client; req.user from middleware outside this repo

trace.note: project loaded from req.store by caller-supplied id, with no ownership filter
authorized(req.user, project) called; it returns a boolean and never throws, and the result is discarded
authorized() defined as a pure predicate returning resource.ownerId === user.id || user.isAdmin === true

finding.guards_checked: authorized() at api.js:12-14 returns a boolean and is not enforced; authorize() at api.js:4-10 throws 403 but is not called on this route (the PUT route at api.js:25 uses it correctly); no ownership guard or middleware in repo; no existence check on project

verdict.guard_found: authorized() at api.js:12-14 is a pure boolean predicate and its result is discarded as a bare statement at api.js:18; authorize() at api.js:4-10 would throw but is not called on the DELETE route (only on PUT at api.js:25); no ownership filter, existence check, or middleware in the repo (only api.js exists in the directory).
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at api.js:18 calls the boolean-returning authorized() and ignores its result, so the delete at api.js:19 runs for any caller-supplied id regardless of ownership; the only enforcing helper, authorize() at api.js:4-10, is not invoked on this route. Attacker is any authenticated low-privilege user (req.user comes from middleware outside this repo), and the flaw grants power beyond their role, so it is a real vulnerability.

finding.claim: Object-existence oracle: a nonexistent id yields a 500 (TypeError on undefined.ownerId) while an existing but unowned id yields a 403, letting a caller enumerate valid project ids. Low confidence and severity.
finding.source: req.params.id (api.js:17 and api.js:24), supplied by the calling client
finding.sink: Response status distinguishes existence: 500 from authorize()/authorized() on undefined (api.js:5, api.js:13) vs 403 at api.js:8

trace.note: PUT route loads project by req.params.id with no existence check
authorize(req.user, undefined) dereferences resource.ownerId and throws TypeError when id is missing
resource.ownerId access in authorize() throws for undefined resource
403 thrown when project exists and ownerId mismatches
same pattern in DELETE route via line 18 authorized() call

finding.guards_checked: No 404 or existence check before the authorization call on either route; no error-handling middleware in repo to normalize status codes

verdict.guard_found: On the PUT route, authorize() (api.js:4-10) throws on mismatch and that throw is not caught, so the 403 vs 500 status split is real. On the DELETE route, authorized() (api.js:12-14) returns a bool that line 18 discards, so it is not a guard at all.
verdict.reason: The trace misdescribes the DELETE route: api.js:17-19 has no 403 path because the bare call to authorized() at api.js:18 discards its boolean, so a non-owner's DELETE of an existing project succeeds with 204 and removes it, which is an authorization bypass rather than an existence oracle. The PUT-route oracle (api.js:24-25 → 500 on undefined at api.js:5 vs 403 at api.js:8) is real, but the finding as written is built on the wrong DELETE trace, so it is refuted in its current form.

finding.claim: Inconsistent admin test: authorize() grants access on a truthy user.isAdmin while authorized() requires strict true. Exploitable only if req.user.isAdmin can be a truthy non-boolean from an unvalidated source; cannot be confirmed from this repo. Low confidence.
finding.source: req.user.isAdmin, populated by middleware outside this repo (not visible)
finding.sink: Authorization decision in authorize() at api.js:5 (PUT /projects/:id/name via api.js:25)

trace.note: authorize() admits request when !user.isAdmin is false, i.e. any truthy isAdmin
authorized() requires isAdmin === true, a stricter test
PUT route relies on authorize() admin semantics

finding.guards_checked: authorized() uses strict equality, which is not applied in authorize(); no type validation of isAdmin in repo; origin of req.user not in repo

verdict.guard_found: No guard in the repo validates isAdmin's type. authorize() at api.js:5 throws only when `!user.isAdmin` is true, so any truthy isAdmin is admitted. authorized() at api.js:13 uses `=== true`, but the PUT route at api.js:25 calls authorize(), not authorized(), so that stricter check does not apply there.
verdict.reason: The trace at api.js:5, :13 and :25 is accurate, but exploitation needs req.user.isAdmin to be a truthy non-boolean, and the middleware that sets req.user is not in this repo, so the precondition cannot be decided here. For boolean isAdmin values, authorize() (api.js:5) and authorized() (api.js:13) behave identically, so there is no in-repo exploit.

finding.claim: Unvalidated write: req.body.name is assigned to the stored project without type or length checks, and the full project record is returned in the response. Impact depends on the store and on rendering code outside this repo. Low confidence.
finding.source: req.body.name (api.js:26), supplied by the authenticated caller in the request body
finding.sink: project.name assignment in req.store-backed object (api.js:26) and res.json(project) (api.js:27)

trace.note: ownership check passes for the owner or admin
raw req.body.name assigned to project.name with no type or length validation
entire project object serialized back to the caller

finding.guards_checked: Ownership check at api.js:25 is correct for this route; no schema validation, body type check, or field whitelist in repo; body parser not in repo

verdict.guard_found: api.js:4-10 `authorize()` throws a 403 when resource.ownerId !== user.id and the user is not an admin. It is called as a bare statement at api.js:25, but because it throws rather than returning a bool, the failure aborts the handler before api.js:26 runs. The other helper, `authorized()` (api.js:12-14), is a different function and is not called on this route.
verdict.reason: The trace matches api.js:25-27, but the only attacker who can reach the write at api.js:26 is the project owner or an admin, who already has the power to rename that project. The ownership guard at api.js:25 (throwing `authorize`, api.js:4-10) blocks everyone else, and the unchecked name is only a data-quality concern, not a privilege or security flaw in this repo.
